definition: A Neural Network Gaussian Process (NNGP) is a Gaussian process (GP) obtained as the limit of a certain type of sequence of neural networks.
details: Specifically, a wide variety of network architectures converges to a GP in the infinitely wide limit, in the sense of distribution. The concept constitutes an intensional definition, i.e., a NNGP is just a GP, but distinguished by how it is obtained.

explainer.lead: It gives an exact probabilistic description of what a neural network becomes when made infinitely wide, turning a hard-to-analyse model into a tractable Gaussian process. This lets researchers reason about uncertainty and generalisation in wide networks using GP theory.

tiers.eli5: Imagine averaging the behaviour of a huge crowd of nearly identical networks; the average behaves like a simple, well-understood statistical object rather than a messy network.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use the NNGP kernel as a fixed, training-free baseline or as the infinite-width limit to compare against finite networks. A common pitfall is assuming finite-width networks behave like the limit, which can be far off at practical widths.
tiers.paperLevel: An NNGP is defined as the distributional limit of a sequence of neural networks as width goes to infinity; the result is a Gaussian process, so the definition is intensional — it is a GP distinguished only by how it arises. It applies in the infinite-width limit, not to finite networks.

explainer.example: A single-hidden-layer network with random weights, as its width grows without bound, converges in distribution to a Gaussian process whose covariance is given by a kernel composed over layers.
